title: Grilled Prawns
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Threaded tail to head so they do not curl, marinated about ten minutes, and cooked in five to eight.
longDesc: The companion to the grilled tilapia, and its one real piece of technique is worth the entry on its own: thread the prawns from tail to head, because this prevents them curling up as they cook. About two pounds of prawns take a quarter cup of grated shallots, a heaping teaspoon each of ginger and garlic, a teaspoon of salt, two teaspoons of dried ground red pepper, a heaping teaspoon of fish spice and four tablespoons of white vegetable oil, with one or two lemons. Ten minutes in the marinade, five to eight minutes to cook.
ingredients: 1 heaping tsp fresh ground or grated ginger
1 tsp fresh garlic, ground, grated or crushed
steps: Peel and devein the prawns if needed.
Mix the grated shallots, ginger, garlic, salt, red pepper, fish spice and oil.
Leave the prawns in the marinade about 10 minutes.
Thread them onto skewers from tail to head — this prevents them curling up as they cook.
They should cook in about 5 to 8 minutes.
Finish with lemon juice and serve.
chefTips: Thread from tail to head. Her own reasoning is that it prevents the prawns curling as they cook, and it is the single most useful prawn-grilling tip anywhere in this collection.
Ten minutes in the marinade, no longer. Prawns take salt and acid very fast and go rubbery if left.
Five to eight minutes total. Prawns are done the moment they turn opaque, so err short.
Fish spice is a Ghanaian market blend rather than a single ingredient and no source lists its composition. Any seafood seasoning will stand in.
Four tablespoons of oil for two pounds of prawns keeps them from sticking to the grill bars.
The lemons are not in the method, only the ingredient list — squeeze them over at the end.
Be aware there is a yield contradiction in the source: one fetch gives six prawns alongside the two-pound weight, which cannot both be right.
commonMistakes: Threading head to tail, so they curl.
Grilling over flames rather than coals.
Forgetting the lemon, which is only in the ingredient list.
sources: Adapted from Recipe #59 within 'Great Grilling: Recipes #58 (Grilled Tilipia) and #59 (Grilled Prawns/Shrimp), and a plea to African entrepreneurs', betumiblog.blogspot.com, timestamped 2011-06-22. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 7:53 PM'. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS) except where noted.

Ingredients exactly as printed: '1/4 cup grated shallots or onion'; '1 heaping teaspoon fresh ground or grated ginger'; '1 teaspoon fresh garlic ground/grated/crushed'; '1 teaspoon salt or seasoning salt'; '2 teaspoons of dried ground red pepper'; '1 heaping teaspoon fish spice'; '4 Tablespoons white vegetable oil'. The 1-2 lemons appeared on one fetch only (SINGLE-PASS).

A YIELD CONTRADICTION, flagged and NOT corrected: one fetch gives a yield of '6 shrimp' alongside 'approximately 2 pounds (or 1 kilo, which is 2.25 pounds)'; the other says only 'for ~2 pounds shrimp'. The '6 shrimp' figure is SINGLE-PASS and conflicts with the weight. The weight is used above and the discrepancy is recorded. Note also that the source's own parenthetical converts 1 kilo to 2.25 pounds, which is correct, while calling it approximately 2 pounds.
TIMES as printed: 'Leave them in the marinade about 10 minutes'. 'They should cook in about 5-8 minutes.'
THE TECHNIQUE, SINGLE-PASS and quoted: thread from tail to head — 'This prevents the shrimp/prawns from curling up as they cook.'
NO SENSORY DONENESS CUE is printed, only the five-to-eight-minute window.
'FISH SPICE' is named as an ingredient with no composition given. It is a Ghanaian market blend and no source consulted lists what is in it. That gap is recorded rather than filled.
THE LEMONS appear in the ingredient list but not in any printed step, so where they go is an editorial reading — at the end, which is the only sensible placement.
The companion tilapia recipe from the same post is published at GHA094.
THE POST'S FULL TITLE includes 'a plea to African entrepreneurs', which is the author's separate argument about African food businesses rather than part of either recipe.
storage: 1 day refrigerated. Grilled prawns do not keep.
reheating: Not recommended — they toughen. Eat cold.
healthBenefits: Prawns are very high in protein and low in fat.
A good source of selenium, iodine and vitamin B12.
culturalNote: Ghana's coast supplies prawns the length of it, and grilled over the same coals as the tilapia they are the quicker half of a beach lunch. Threading tail to head so they stay straight is the kind of small, practical knowledge that distinguishes someone who has grilled a lot of prawns from someone who has read about it.
